home.title: SentinelDesk — A collaborative operating system for people and AI agents
home.h1: A collaborative operating system for people and AI agents
home.lede: A complete Linux desktop running inside a container with no physical monitor, streamed to the browser over WebRTC — and driven, at the same time, by people and by an agent that sees and acts on the same screen. Same X display, same session, same room.
home.note: Published here, in three languages. The desktop's Docs button opens this same guide.
home.demo.chip.ask: AI agent is asking for control
home.demo.cap: A loop of the turn-taking, not a live session. While a person is connected the agent has to ask, and the answer is theirs to give; with an empty room it simply works, because there is nobody to take turns with.
home.planes.h2: Two independent control planes over one desktop
home.planes.p: The second half is not a metaphor for an API. A person drives through a control layer in the browser; an agent drives through a local Unix socket. Neither is a guest of the other, and that separation is the single most important thing about the design.
home.c1.p: /ws is the only door. The first frame must be an authentication frame; until it validates there is no SDP offer, no ICE and no DataChannel. Keyboard and mouse arrive on a data channel and go into X through XTEST.
home.c2.p: A 0600 Unix socket exposes 114 tools to any MCP-capable host. The bridge is a thin stdio pipe spawned with docker exec, so killing the host never takes the desktop down with it.
home.arch.p1: Pion WebRTC and GStreamer live in one process: every RTP packet goes from appsink straight onto the WebRTC track, and the encoder stays under full control at runtime — bitrate changes, keyframes on demand, stream destinations attached and detached without cutting anything.
home.arch.p2: At startup it probes NVENC, VA-API, x264 and VP8 with a real pipeline and keeps the first that works on that host. Congestion control over TWCC — the same technique Google Meet uses — steers the bitrate, and the pointer is drawn on the client, so perceived latency is about zero. Typical: 50–70 ms glass-to-glass on a LAN.
home.arch.alt: SentinelDesk architecture: the container's X display captured once by GStreamer, encoded and fanned out over WebRTC to several browsers, with a parallel MCP control plane over a local Unix socket.
home.arch.cap: Capture, encode and fan-out, with the two control planes either side.
home.quick.h2: One command on a machine of its own
home.quick.p: The installer downloads one binary and asks it for everything else: the binary embeds its own deployment files, so configuration and code can never disagree about versions. auto picks Docker when it is present and a native systemd install otherwise.
home.quick.pre: # VPS or Raspberry Pi 5 (Debian 13 / Raspberry Pi OS) curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/\ lordbasex/sentineldesk/main/install.sh | sudo bash -s auto # or, from a clone, for development make up # → http://localhost:8080
home.quick.note: Set AUTH_USER and AUTH_PASS before exposing it. Without them authentication is disabled, which is for LAN development only.
home.final.h2: Put a person and an agent on the same screen
home.final.p: Everything is in one repository, under Apache 2.0: the daemon, the browser client, the deployment tree and the installer.
arch.title: Architecture — SentinelDesk
arch.lede: Everything else follows from that separation: people come in over a WebSocket, the agent over a local Unix socket, and neither is a guest of the other.
arch.alt: SentinelDesk architecture diagram: the container's X display captured once by GStreamer, encoded and fanned out over WebRTC to several browsers, with the MCP control plane in parallel over a local Unix socket.
arch.cap: Capture, encode and fan-out, with the two control planes either side. Note: the diagram is labelled 106 tools; the current catalogue has 114.
arch.desktop.p1: Xvfb :0 provides a virtual display with no physical monitor behind it. Openbox manages window frames and nothing else — it does not draw the desktop. That job belongs to pcmanfm in desktop mode, which owns the root window and paints the wallpaper and icons, with lxpanel on top.
arch.desktop.p2: Everything runs under supervisord, so any piece restarts on its own without taking the rest down: xvfb, pulseaudio, dbus-session, at-spi, openbox, pcmanfm-desktop, lxpanel and sentineldesk itself.
arch.video.p1: ximagesrc reads the framebuffer and hands it to GStreamer, which runs inside the Go process through go-gst rather than as a separate gst-launch child. That is what keeps the encoder reachable while it runs: bitrate changes, keyframes on demand, and destinations attached and detached without cutting anything.
arch.video.p2: The encoder is chosen at startup by running a real probe pipeline for each candidate, in order. The choice reflects what actually works on that host, not what the drivers claim to support.
arch.video.p3: Encoded frames leave through an appsink and each RTP packet goes straight onto the Pion track. On the H.264 encoders they also pass through a tee: in the normal case nothing is attached to it, and that is where an external destination gets a copy of the same picture the room is already receiving. Streaming to YouTube does not mean encoding the screen a second time.
arch.tee.note: Why the tee sits before h264parse. Each branch parses for itself: WebRTC wants byte-stream and FLV wants AVC. Asking one parser to produce both deadlocks the negotiation. Parsing is nearly free — it reads headers, it does not decode — so the duplication costs nothing next to a second encoder.
arch.audio.p: There is no sound card, so PulseAudio loads a null sink named sentineldesk. Applications play into it and pulsesrc sentineldesk.monitor captures what they played; opusenc encodes it and a second appsink feeds the audio track.
arch.mic.p1: The browser's microphone travels the other way, and the return path needs two PulseAudio objects rather than one:
arch.mic.pre:
incoming Opus track → appsrc → pulsesink device=sentineldesk_mic
                             → null sink "sentineldesk_mic"
                               → sentineldesk_mic.monitor
                                 → module-remap-source "sentineldesk_mic_in"
arch.mic.p2: The remap is not decoration. A monitor is how PulseAudio exposes "what a sink is playing", and applications treat it as such: browsers list monitors separately from real inputs, or hide them from the microphone picker altogether. Remapped, the same audio presents as an ordinary capture device — and it is made the system default.
arch.mic.p3: Both objects are created at startup, not on first use. A page enumerates its audio devices when it loads, so a microphone that appears later is missing from the list of the very page that wanted it.
arch.human.p1: WS /ws is the only door. The first frame must be {type:"auth"}; until it validates there is no SDP offer, no ICE, no DataChannel. After authentication the same socket carries signalling and presence.
arch.human.p2: HTTP :8080 serves the client embedded with go:embed and the file-manager endpoints, and holds no secrets: the ICE configuration and TURN credentials travel over the already-authenticated WebSocket. The only informational endpoint is /auth, which says nothing beyond whether a login is required. There is no /login endpoint, by design: HTTP is not the authentication gate.
arch.human.p3: Keyboard and mouse arrive over a DataChannel named input and are injected into X through XTEST. A browser gamepad becomes a virtual Xbox 360 pad through uinput, where the host exposes /dev/uinput.
arch.agent.h2: Control plane 2 — the agent, over a local Unix socket
arch.agent.p1: The MCP server listens on /run/user/1000/sentineldesk-mcp.sock, mode 0600, and exposes 114 tools. The AI host spawns sentineldesk -mcp-stdio with docker exec; that sub-command is a thin JSON-RPC pipe between stdin/stdout and the socket. Killing the host never takes the desktop down with it.
arch.agent.p2: Two helper bridges cover what pixels cannot: a11y.py exposes the AT-SPI accessibility tree (the ui_* tools, which invoke a button by name rather than by coordinates) and Chromium runs with CDP on port 9222 (the browser_* tools, which drive the real DOM).
arch.agent.p3: What the agent may do is bounded by a three-level policy — full, safe, readonly — plus a denylist and an allowlist. The daemon sets the ceiling through the environment, and each connection can restrict itself further but never widen.
arch.pol.safe: Everything except running code or touching the system; as_root is out
arch.pol.readonly: Observation only: see the screen, read the tree, list things
arch.room.h2: The room, and one deliberate asymmetry
arch.room.p1: Capture happens once and is fanned out to up to four participants (MAX_VIEWERS), so a second viewer does not cost a second encoder. One person drives at a time; the rest watch, and control is handed over cooperatively: everyone arrived with the same credential, so there is no hierarchy to enforce.
arch.room.p2: The shared encoder's bitrate is the minimum of what each network estimates, because encoding for the best link would drop the worst one.
arch.room.p3: Each participant's pointer is drawn as a real X window, not as an overlay in each browser. That distinction matters: because the pointer is part of the desktop, it appears in recordings, in screenshots and in every other viewer's stream, instead of existing only in one browser's DOM.
arch.asym: The asymmetry, stated plainly: MCP tools do not go through the room's control arbitration. They inject straight into XTEST, because the MCP arrives over the daemon's local socket rather than over the web. Arbitration exists between browsers. To stop an agent from touching anything, the instrument is its policy (-mcp-policy readonly), not room control.
arch.net.p1: On Linux with network_mode: host, ICE connects directly over UDP with nothing in between — the fastest path. On macOS and Windows the Docker Desktop VM breaks direct ICE, so deploy/docker-compose.yml includes coturn as a relay. For clients behind strict corporate NAT, publish coturn in production too and pass its URLs through CLIENT_TURN_URLS.
arch.net.p2: If the server sits behind NAT and does not hold the public IP on its own interface, set NAT1TO1_IP=<public IP> so ICE advertises the right address.
arch.code.pre:
cmd/sentineldesk/   wiring only: flags, HTTP, WebSocket, MCP socket
internal/config/    environment configuration
internal/desktop/   X11: input injection, cursor, clipboard, joystick, pointers
internal/media/     GStreamer: pipelines, encoders, recording, upstream audio
internal/stream/    sessions, the shared room, auth, rate limiting, TLS, files
internal/mcp/       the MCP server and its 114 tools
internal/webui/     the browser client, embedded with go:embed
deploy/             Dockerfile, compose, desktop and supervisor config
arch.code.p: The backend is a single Go binary (Pion WebRTC + go-gst). Because it uses CGO to link GStreamer, it cannot be cross-compiled with a bare GOOS/GOARCH: release binaries are built inside the Debian 13 Docker stage and extracted, so they are byte-for-byte what the container runs.
install.title: Installation — SentinelDesk
install.h1: A binary that brings its own deployment
install.lede: The installer downloads one binary and asks it for everything else. The binary embeds its own deployment files, so configuration and code can never disagree about versions: there is no second download to fall out of step with.
install.own.h2: On a machine of its own
install.own.p1: For a VPS or a Raspberry Pi 5 (Debian 13 / Raspberry Pi OS, amd64 or arm64):
install.own.p2: auto picks Docker when it is present and a native systemd install otherwise; docker or native choose explicitly. A running binary can also hand its files to another machine: sentineldesk -install serves them over HTTP and sentineldesk -extract-deploy <dir> writes them to disk.
install.own.note: Every build knows what it is: sentineldesk -version prints something like sentineldesk v1.2.3 (081b14d) · build 20260804-190000, and the same string appears at the bottom of the control rail.
install.dev.pre: make up # build the image and start the desktop make logs # follow the logs make shell # a root shell inside the container make down # stop everything
install.dev.p: Then http://localhost:8080. With AUTH_USER and AUTH_PASS set it asks for a login; without them it is open, and that is for development only.
install.prod.p: Pick the compose file that matches the server's hardware. All three use network_mode: host for a direct ICE connection, which is the lowest latency.
install.prod.pre: # CPU only (software VP8) AUTH_USER=admin AUTH_PASS=secret \ docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.cpu.yml up -d # NVIDIA GPU (NVENC) — needs nvidia-container-toolkit AUTH_USER=admin AUTH_PASS=secret \ docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.nvidia.yml up -d # Intel/AMD GPU (VA-API) — passes /dev/dri through AUTH_USER=admin AUTH_PASS=secret \ docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.vaapi.yml up -d
install.prod.warn: Before exposing it to the internet, always set AUTH_USER and AUTH_PASS: the production compose files require them. Without them authentication is disabled, which is good for a development LAN and for nothing else.
install.tls.p: Two ways to serve HTTPS, depending on whether you have a proxy in front.
install.tls.a.h3: A. Native TLS in the backend
install.tls.self: Generates a self-signed certificate once and persists it in the volume. SANs: localhost, the hostname, plus whatever you add in TLS_HOSTS=ip,domain. Good for a LAN or for testing.
install.tls.own: Uses your own certificate: a purchased wildcard, a corporate one, or one issued by certbot. Copy the files into deploy/certs/, which is mounted as /certs.
install.tls.pre: TLS_SELFSIGNED=1 docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d # → https://localhost:8080
install.tls.b.h3: B. Caddy as a reverse proxy
install.tls.b.p: With --profile tls on the production compose files, choosing the mode with TLS_MODE=.
install.tls.ss.n: Nothing: works by IP or local name
install.tls.pre2: # Classic Let's Encrypt DOMAIN=desktop.example.com AUTH_USER=admin AUTH_PASS=secret \ docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.nvidia.yml --profile tls up -d # Self-signed through Caddy (no domain) TLS_MODE=selfsigned AUTH_USER=admin AUTH_PASS=secret \ docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.cpu.yml --profile tls up -d
install.tls.p2: In any of these modes the WebSocket switches to wss:// on its own. Ports to open in the firewall: 80/443 for the web, and WebRTC's UDP range (or the fixed one you set with WEBRTC_MIN_PORT / WEBRTC_MAX_PORT).
install.vars.p: Configuration is environment-only: the container is the unit of deployment, and a separate configuration file would just be one more thing that can disagree with the compose file.
install.v.fps: Frames per second (60 is worth it with a GPU)
install.v.vbr: Bitrate ceiling; the adaptive loop only goes lower
install.v.cur: 1 draws the pointer on the server (more perceived latency)
install.v.max: How many people share one desktop
install.v.secret: HMAC key for session tokens; pin it to survive restarts
install.v.files: How far the file manager may reach
install.v.nat: Public IP to advertise in ICE (server behind NAT)
install.v.port: Port for the web client and signalling
install.mcp.p1: The bridge runs inside the container, so the AI host launches it with docker exec. In the host's MCP configuration:
install.mcp.li1: -i keeps stdin open: that is the MCP transport.
install.mcp.li2: -u sentineldesk runs as the socket's owner (uid 1000).
install.mcp.li3: The container has to be named sentineldesk, or adjust the name.
install.mcp.p2: To hand an agent a read-only endpoint against the same daemon you use with full permissions, add -mcp-policy readonly to those arguments. A connection can drop below the ceiling the daemon set, never raise it.
install.steps.h2: Getting it running, end to end
install.st1.p: Whichever compose file matches the hardware, with AUTH_USER and AUTH_PASS set.
install.st2.p: Port 8080 by default. Whoever arrives first takes control; the rest watch and can ask for it.
install.st3.h3: Add TLS if it faces the internet
install.st3.p: Native TLS with TLS_SELFSIGNED=1, or Caddy with --profile tls and a domain.
install.st4.p: The MCP bridge over docker exec, with whatever policy you want to give it.
install.final.p: The full user guide, in three languages — the same one the desktop's rail links to.
home.idea.h2: Not a metaphor for an API
home.idea.p: The agent is not handed a screenshot service or a headless browser. It joins the same X display, the same session, the same room as the people — with a seat of its own.
home.idea.c1.p: It has a name in the participant list and a pointer on screen in its own colour, so it is never ambiguous whether a colleague or the model just moved the mouse.
home.idea.c2.p: Exactly one participant holds control. While a person is connected the agent has to ask — a prompt with a timer appears on their screen, and no answer means no. With an empty room it simply works.
home.idea.c3.p: Every command run in a terminal reports its exit status, whoever ran it. A person can hit an error, ask the agent to look, and the agent reads what actually happened instead of being told about it.
home.idea.c4.p: The desktop is encoded once and fanned out — to every browser, to the recorder, to a live stream. A second participant costs bandwidth, not CPU.
home.side.you.h3: From the rail, a person can
home.side.you.li1: Take and release control — handover is cooperative, and whoever arrives first drives
home.side.you.li2: Send their microphone into the desktop, where it appears as a real capture device
home.side.you.li3: Take screenshots and record to MP4, WebM or MKV
home.side.you.li4: Stream the live session to YouTube, Twitch or their own VLC/OBS
home.side.you.li5: Move files both ways with a two-pane manager, share the clipboard, plug in a gamepad
home.side.you.li6: Watch live statistics and read the documentation in three languages
home.side.agent.li1: Move the mouse and type; manage windows, desktops and processes
home.side.agent.li2: Open a terminal the person can watch — and read back what happened, exit codes included
home.side.agent.li3: Read the screen as an accessibility tree or drive Chromium through DevTools: structure, not pixels
home.side.agent.li4: Read and write files, install packages, open shells and SSH sessions with tunnels
home.side.agent.li5: Take snapshots it can roll back to
home.side.agent.li6: Ask the room for its turn — and accept no for an answer
home.t1.p: Hardware encoding picked by a real probe, keyframes on demand when a frame is lost, adaptive bitrate that follows what the network actually gives, and a minimal jitter buffer. Latency over smoothness, on purpose.
home.t2.p: Authentication happens on the WebSocket: until it validates there is no WebRTC handshake at all. No HTTP endpoint holds secrets, repeated failures feed an escalating ban ledger, and sessions ride an HMAC-signed token.
home.t3.p: Chromium, VLC, a terminal, a file manager, TigerVNC, FreeRDP and Steam on Debian 13 — amd64 and arm64, from a bare VPS to a Raspberry Pi 5.
home.rail.p: People drive the desktop through a single instrument rail floating over the video. Its left edge always answers the first question — who is driving: solid green means you, hatched amber means somebody else.
home.rail.cap: The rail as it ships: 240 px expanded, 58 px collapsed to icons, hidden entirely with the º key.
home.rail.a1.p: The hero module: how many are connected and who holds control. When it is not you, the module turns amber and hatched, and “Take control” asks for your turn — handover is cooperative. The strip on the rail's left edge repeats the answer at a glance: solid green, you drive.
home.rail.a2.p: Sends your voice into the desktop, where it appears as a real capture device — and the system default. Right-click picks which microphone. Only whoever holds control publishes.
home.rail.a3.p: Saves a picture of the screen to your machine; an agent can ask for the same shot left on the container's disk instead.
home.rail.a4.p: MP4, WebM or MKV, reusing the encode the room is already producing. While it runs, a REC pill with the elapsed time is visible to everyone.
home.rail.a5.p: A two-pane manager — remote desktop on the left, your machine on the right — with Midnight Commander keys: F5 copy, F6 rename, F7 mkdir, F8 delete. Dropping files anywhere on the page copies them to the desktop.
home.rail.a6.p: The desktop's sound in your browser; one click mutes it.
home.rail.a7.p: The live WebRTC readout of the connection you are on: bitrate, FPS, latency and packet loss.
home.rail.a8.p: The desktop at full size, with the rail still floating over it. In this demo it opens a simulated desktop: the Openbox panel, Chromium showing the project page, and a terminal typing by itself. Drag the windows by their title bars — Esc to come back.
home.rail.a9.p: EN · ES · PT. The choice follows you into the documentation, which opens in the same language.
home.rail.a10.p: Clears the session token and returns to the front door.
home.rail.a11.p: The rail collapses to a 58 px column of icons, or vanishes entirely with the º key; a discreet handle on the screen edge brings it back.
home.shots.h2: The desktop, as you will see it
home.shots.s1: Watching mode: a video playing in Chromium with sound in your browser, one press away from taking the controls
home.shots.s2: The AI agent asking for control — Allow or Refuse, with the timer draining; silence refuses
home.shots.s3: The two-pane file manager over the desktop — remote on the left, your machine on the right — with the live WebRTC readout in the corner
home.shots.s4: The controls are free: htop watching the desktop's own processes, and whoever presses “Take control” drives
home.rail.l.watchHtml: You are watching — press “Take control” to interact
home.rail.t.hidden: Rail hidden — press º or the edge handle to bring it back
home.rail.fm.drop: Drop files here to send them to the desktop
home.rail.a12.p: Sends this desktop to YouTube, Twitch, Facebook — or to a VLC/OBS of your own over udp:// or srt:// — reusing the encode the room is already producing. A LIVE chip on the rail stays visible to everyone while anything is being sent.
home.rail.a13.p: Opens this same guide in a new tab, in the language the rail is set to.
home.rail.rs.title: Live streaming
home.rail.rs.hintCustom: Point VLC or OBS at this machine. From Docker the host is host.docker.internal. Use udp:// for VLC — it only speaks srt:// as a caller, so it cannot receive one. srt:// is for a receiver that listens.
home.rail.rs.kfNote: Off, the picture stays sharper: keyframes are large and the bits they take come out of the detail. Platforms always get them.
